document.title: 2026-09-03 Final EQIX IRAS Comments
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE  
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
) 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.  
 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3515 
 
 
) 
 
PROTEST, REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION AND  
COMMENTS OF EQUINIX INC. ON THE  
PROPOSAL OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C. TO  
ESTABLISH INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE AND A  
LARGE LOAD REGISTRY TO ADDRESS SYSTEM RELIABILITY 
 
Equinix Inc. (“Equinix”) appreciates this opportunity to contribute its protest, request for 
clarification and comments in response to the filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) 
entitled “Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service and a Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability” (the “IRAS Filing”), which 
PJM submitted on August 13, 2026.1  We respectfully provide this submission for consideration 
by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) pursuant to Rule 
211 of its Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, and the Commission’s notice 
issued in this docket.2  
I. 
SUMMARY 
Consistent with its own U.S. Community Principles,3 and as a signatory to the Ratepayer 
Protection Pledge, Equinix supports the general principle behind the IRAS Filing: that new large 
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., “Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim Resource 
Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability,” Docket No. ER26-3515-000, 
Transmittal Letter (August 13, 2026) (“IRAS Transmittal”). Capitalized terms not defined herein have the meanings 
given in the Transmittal, the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”), or the PJM Reliability 
Assurance Agreement among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”). 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Combined Notice of Filings, (Aug. 13, 2026) 
(establishing a comment date of Sept. 3, 2026). Equinix filed a timely doc-less motion to intervene in this 
proceeding on Aug. 21, 2026.. 
3 Available at https://equinixtogether.com/community-principles/.

2 
loads should bear the obligation to bring sufficient new capacity to the system to meet its needs, 
and that those who have not procured new capacity should bear curtailment risk during periods 
of grid stress. The alternative would unjustly shift that risk resulting from the pressure new large 
load growth places on system resources on other customers.4 
Equinix appreciates that objective, and PJM’s intent to achieve it. The IRAS Filing’s 
approach unfortunately and unnecessarily blurs the jurisdictional line between federal and state 
authority, creating complexities and uncertainties that undermine the very objective it is meant to 
serve: to have large loads procure new capacity. As explained below, this approach makes it very 
difficult for large loads to procure new capacity with any confidence that doing so will protect 
them from IRAS curtailment or Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”)5 cost allocation. 
Equinix accordingly protests and seeks clarification of four targeted aspects of the IRAS 
Filing. First, the definitions of Large Load and New Large Load fail to protect loads already 
under final retail service contracts, which would effectively override those contracts and the 
financial expectations built on them— and which would be particularly damaging for facilities 
that have already commenced energization. Second, the one-mile aggregation rule improperly 
treats independently developed legacy facilities as a single electrical site based on distance alone, 
without regard to long-standing legitimate commercial reasons for siting that have no relation to 
energy. Third, Schedule 11 permits PJM to rely on Large Load Registry information without 
requiring notice to, verification by, or a meaningful correction process for the affected Large 
Load. Fourth, Equinix seeks clarification, or in the alternative protests, PJM’s failure to credit a 
verified, customer-sponsored Peak Shaving Adjustments on a basis comparable to other 
 
4 IRAS Filing at 4–5 & n.10 (identifying Equinix, Inc. among the data centers that have joined the 
Ratepayer Protection Pledge). 
5 PJM’s RBP proposal is before the Commission in Docket ER26-3380.

3 
investments that address the same resource-adequacy need.. 
Equinix therefore asks that FERC take the following actions to avoid otherwise unjust 
and unreasonable results: 
1) Revise the definition of “New Large Load” to exclude any load including a 
contractual ramp, covered by a binding retail service (including transmission 
service or electric service) agreement executed before August 13, 2026, the date 
of the IRAS filing, so as not to override existing contracts and the financial 
expectations built on them.  
 
2) Revise the definition of “large load” to eliminate the one-mile aggregation radius, 
which PJM adapted from Qualified Facility (“QF”) siting rules without 
meaningful stakeholder input or a reasoned account of how data centers differ 
from QFs. In the alternative, if the Commission finds that geographic aggregation 
of existing facilities may be just and reasonable in some circumstances, we ask 
that it direct PJM to make the one-mile rule a rebuttable presumption, allowing a 
customer to show that affiliated facilities are separate sites based on factors such 
as separate service arrangements, points of interconnection, ownership and 
control, development history, or electrical and operational independence.6 
 
3) Amend Schedule 11 to require PJM to provide each Large Load notice of the 
information attributed to it, a meaningful opportunity to correct or supplement 
that information before PJM relies on it, and a prompt process to resolve disputes 
over New Large Load status, registered peak load, capacity coverage, and related 
Large Load Registry determinations. 
 
4)  Revise the Tariff so that a New Large Load receives credit comparable to 
BYONC when it funds a qualifying Peak Shaving Adjustment that reduces PJM’s 
capacity need, whether at its own site or provided by other customers. The credit 
should reflect the reduction recognized by PJM and reduce the load’s IRAS 
obligation, subject to verification and protections against double counting. 
 
I. BACKGROUND AND INTEREST OF EQUINIX 
Equinix, based in Redwood City, California, is one of the oldest and largest data center 
developers in the world, with data centers across six continents, over 35 countries, and more than 
70 metropolitan areas. The data centers Equinix develops, owns and operates are long-lived 
 
6 See Qualifying Facility Rates and Requirements Implementation Issues Under the Public Utility 
Regulatory Policies Act of 1978, Order No. 872, 172 FERC ¶ 61,041, order on reh’g & clarifying in part, Order No. 
872-A, 173 FERC ¶ 61,158 (2020); IRAS Filing at 33 & n.95 (citing Order No. 872 as the analog for PJM’s one-
mile radius rule, which the Commission applies as an irrebuttable presumption for QF siting).

4 
assets developed against investment horizons measured in decades rather than quarters. We 
develop two distinct types of data centers: colocation data centers, which we call International 
Business Exchanges (or “IBXs”) and house as many as 400 separate customers, and larger data 
centers, which we call “xScale” facilities, which generally house one or two customers. 
Private enterprises, network operators, cloud providers, governmental entities and 
nonprofits house computing equipment and interconnect with one another and with the broader 
internet within Equinix’s International Business Exchange (“IBX”) data centers. Many of 
Equinix’s customers utilize the computing equipment in our data centers and the data 
interconnection services we provide to enable critical services, such as emergency response, grid 
operations, medical information, and national security. Each individual IBX facility may house 
as many as 400 co-located customers. Our IBX data centers range between a few megawatts up 
to approximately 100 MW, and average in the mid-30 MWs.  
Equinix also develops, owns and operates larger xScale data centers, which can exceed 
750 MW. Our xScale data centers generally serve one or two customers, each of which requires  
a significant dedicated proportion, or even the entirety, of these larger facilities.  
Equinix has operated in the PJM Region for decades. Its facilities include the very first 
commercial data center in Data Center Alley in Northern Virginia, as well as many other data 
centers in that area and elsewhere in Northern Virginia; numerous data centers in the Chicago 
area; and numerous data centers in  New Jersey. Equinix takes retail electric service from 
Electric Distributors and Load Serving Entities across the PJM Region and, in retail choice 
jurisdictions, procures its supply through competitive retail suppliers. Depending on how 
Equinix’s procurement of new capacity is credited, Equinix could be directly affected by IRAS 
load-reduction obligations. Equinix has no financial interest in the outcome of the IRAS as a

5 
provider of capacity; its interest is entirely as a developer, owner and operator of large loads. 
Equinix has always held itself to a high standard of care for the communities it operates 
in. Recognizing that more is needed to meet the current moment, Equinix recently memorialized 
its practices explicitly through its U.S. Community Principles.7  These principles include 
Equinix’s commitment to power responsibility, ensuring it “pays the full cost of its grid 
infrastructure needs so costs are not passed to consumers.”8 Equinix does not regard the 
reliability consequences of large load growth as someone else’s problem to solve, and it has 
committed capital to the long-term arrangements needed for new generating capacity and energy 
infrastructure. 
Equinix’s interest in this proceeding is in the long-term stability, predictability, and 
durability of the rules that govern reliability and market conditions, including resource adequacy, 
across the PJM Region. As a load that intends to sign long-term supply commitments, Equinix 
needs to know what those commitments will provide, what risks will remain, and how to best 
address those remaining risks. That is the lens through which Equinix offers the comments that 
follow. 
II.  DISCUSSION 
A. WHEN THE ROLLERSKATES AND THE KEY AREN’T SHARED, NO 
ONE HAS ANY FUN: THE LACK OF COORDINATION BETWEEN 
WHOLESALE AND RETAIL RULES UNDERMINES LARGE LOAD 
CAPACITY PROCUREMENT 
While Equinix does not take a position on the jurisdictional questions raised by PJM’s 
approach, the Commission should be aware of the practical, commercial effect of an approach 
that raises those questions, which is to undermines the ability of new large loads to procure new 
 
7 Available at https://equinixtogether.com/community-principles/.  
8 Id.

6 
capacity with confidence. PJM could have chosen at least two paths that would have better 
avoided this problem, but took neither.  
Under what might be termed a “tough love” approach, PJM could have confined itself to 
the responsibilities that are clearly at the federal wholesale level —assessing whether the 
aggregate new large load reported by PJM-jurisdictional entities is matched by aggregate new 
capacity, procuring against any gap through the RBP, and directing zonal load reductions when 
the gap persists during grid stress. This would leave the states, exercising their jurisdiction over 
the retail service, to define, coordinate, and enforce customer-level procurement and curtailment 
rules.  
Under an approach that truly maximized “cooperative federalism,” PJM could instead 
have convened with state authorities to align definitions and implementation mechanisms before 
filing. While this would be challenging, it would have given load and capacity providers a more 
coherent foundation on which to contract-- with greater certainty, lower cost and lower risk. 
Instead, the IRAS Filing has waded into matters that are at best gray areas for federal 
jurisdiction and at worst squarely within state jurisdiction. Through the Large Load and New 
Large Load definitions and the Large Load Registry, PJM has taken on the task of deciding 
whether a retail load is new, whether it is one facility or several, and whether—and how much—
new capacity it has procured, rather than simply ensuring that the aggregate load and aggregate 
new capacity is reported to PJM properly and accurately. PJM’s own view that its procurement 
determination is nonbinding on Electric Distributors9 offers new large loads no real comfort: it 
means that satisfying PJM’s definitions carries no guarantee of protection from curtailment, 
while satisfying state procurement requirements may still leave a load looking, on paper, like it 
 
9 IRAS Filing at p. 86, but cf. IRAS Filing at p. 41, which appears at least somewhat contradictory; PJM is 
making a determination, but then claims that determination has no actual impact of that determination.

7 
failed to procure. As explained below, that is far from saying the Large Load Registry would 
have no value. To the contrary, as PJM points out, stakeholders generally supported the 
concept.10  It simply underlines the importance of having determinations affecting retail load 
made by those entities with jurisdiction over that load.  The tremendous value that the Large 
Load Registry offers, of collecting the relevant facts from entities with jurisdiction over retail 
load in a central repository, would remain.11 
Equinix has been actively engaged in procurement of new capacity, but is frankly 
frustrated with the lack of clarity that has complicated transactions, increased their risk and 
thereby increased their cost- resulting in an unnecessary drag on both the energy and data 
economies so important to the Nation. Since PJM’s Board first introduced the Critical Issue Fast 
Path (“CIFP”) process for large load additions in August 2025, Equinix has understood the 
direction of policy at every jurisdictional level to be pointing toward one goal: “new” large loads 
procuring supply from “new” capacity resources. Equinix did not wait for every detail of that 
policy to be settled.  It quickly began to seek bilateral procurement intended to satisfy whatever 
framework eventually emerged. Defining that obligation with enough precision to contract 
against it has, much to the detriment of the shared objectives, proven difficult for the reasons that 
follow.12 
Equinix has several projects with energization dates in 2028, 2029, and beyond we view 
as “new.” It also has many facilities that have been energized for years and continue to grow 
through ordinary customer changes and from the multi-year ramp schedules typical of data 
 
10 IRAS Filing at p. 30-31. 
11 Cf. IRAS Filing at p. 67, for example, with the calculations PJM anticipates performing as discussed at 
pp. 113 et seq. 
12 See IRAS Filing at 13 & n.33 (citing Letter of David E. Mills, PJM Board Chair, PJM Board Letter 
Implementing CIFP for Large Load Additions (Aug. 8, 2025)).

8 
center energization. PJM’s discussion makes clear that it intends load added through a facility’s 
ramp after June 1, 2027, to be treated as “New Large Load.” The Large Load Registry would 
include the in-service date for each increment of load, as well as the facility’s peak load and 
ramp schedule, and PJM describes the in-service date of each increment as critical to 
determining IRAS applicability. The proposed tariff language, however, does not clearly 
implement that intent.  
Clause (b) of the New Large Load definition applies to incremental load that enters 
service after June 1, 2027, and increases the load at a site that, before that increment, did not 
meet the Large Load definition. Read literally, that language appears to capture the increment 
that causes a previously smaller site to cross the 50 MW threshold, but not subsequent 
increments at a site that already meets the Large Load definition. It also does not clearly state 
whether the New Large Load consists only of the qualifying increment or the entire registered 
peak load of the site.  
That ambiguity has direct consequences for Equinix. A facility energized in 2023, 2024, 
or 2025 may continue to ramp after June 1, 2027, under a retail service agreement that was 
negotiated, studied, and executed years earlier. PJM’s discussion indicates that it intends to treat 
the post-June 1, 2027, portion of that ramp as new, even though the utility may already have 
committed to serve the facility’s full ramp. Yet the proposed tariff does not clearly identify 
which increments would be treated as New Large Load or how the corresponding MW obligation 
would be calculated. Equinix therefore cannot determine with confidence the amount of BYONC 
it would need to procure. The Commission should require PJM to clarify the definition and, more 
importantly, exclude ramp increments covered by binding retail service agreements executed 
before the IRAS Filing.

9 
Even the “clear” cases of new load raise open questions: must a New Large Load procure 
capacity equal to its ultimate peak load contribution, or the design capacity it originally 
requested from its Electric Distributor? Must it procure that full amount from the first day of 
service, or may it ramp its procurement alongside its ramping demand? PJM’s proposal to collect 
load and BYONC ramp schedules, and to permit BYONC in excess of a load’s current Eligible 
New Large Load Amount, suggests that procurement may track expected growth. But the 
proposed tariff does not say how PJM will translate those schedules into the registered peak load 
used to calculate the facility’s IRAS obligation. Customers served by a vertically integrated 
Electric Distributor are left with this question: has that utility’s procurement of qualifying new 
capacity through its own supply plan already satisfied some or all of the customer’s BYONC 
obligation?  
PJM has relied on the Large Load Adjustment to assess the magnitude and timing of 
large load growth that it contends requires the measures proposed here. Yet neither Equinix nor 
its Electric Distributor can determine how individual facilities are reflected in that adjustment. 
Equinix knows what information it provides to its Electric Distributor, but not what the Electric 
Distributor ultimately submit to PJM. PJM, in turn, has made adjustments to the Electric 
Distributor submissions before the Large Load Adjustments are finalized in a forecast. PJM 
explained in the stakeholder process that the Large Load Adjustments cannot identify how an 
individual load site is reflected or whether or not it is included in the final load forecast. That 
opacity now has direct consequences because customers cannot determine which facilities and 
ramp increments PJM will treat as in service by June 1, 2027, and therefore would be outside the 
definition of New large Load, and which PJM will subject to IRAS. Placing large load 
information in a new Large Load Registry will not resolve this problem if PJM uses that

10 
information through the same opaque process, without allowing an affected customer to see and 
correct its facility’s classification, registered peak load, and ramp schedule.  
 This lack of transparency is not merely administrative. It prevents Equinix from 
identifying the amount and timing of its IRAS obligation and, in turn, from reliably negotiating 
the long-term, high-value bilateral commitments BYONC requires. Even if PJM recognizes a 
particular capacity arrangement as BYONC, that determination does not establish how the 
relevant Electric Distributor or state authorities will treat the customer for purposes of retail 
curtailment or the allocation of RBP costs. Equinix therefore could make a substantial long-term 
commitment without assurance that it will receive the protection from IRAS curtailment and 
RBP cost allocation that gives the commitment its value.  
A workable framework would require greater coordination between PJM and the states 
because PJM cannot unilaterally determine the retail consequences of a customer’s capacity 
procurement. Had PJM better coordinated with state authorities to develop complementary 
definitions and mechanisms before imposing these obligations, large loads and capacity 
providers would have had a more coherent foundation for least-cost, least-risk contracting. The 
Large Load Registry could then have served as a genuinely useful, customer-verified source of 
information—helping PJM, Electric Distributors, and state authorities apply their respective rules 
using a common set of facts and better enabled avoid double-counting across both wholesale and 
retail regimes, in accordance with respective jurisdictional limits. Instead, the proposed Large 
Load Registry would collect information about individual retail facilities and contracts without 
ensuring that affected customers can verify that information or that qualifying BYONC will 
receive consistent treatment under the applicable retail rules- and PJM has proposed taking it 
upon itself to calculate results based on that information.

11 
B.  PJM SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED TO VIOLATE TERMS AND 
CONDITIONS OF EXISTING RETAIL SERVICE CONTRACTS  
PJM is a world-leading wholesale market operator, but data centers (and other retail load) 
are not wholesale customers- just as all fasteners are not nails, notwithstanding the perspective of 
the proverbial carpenter. The further PJM strays from its wholesale market swim lane, the more 
numerous and severe the problems it inadvertently creates.  
PJM’s proposed Large Load and New Large Load definitions would attach new resource-
adequacy and curtailment consequences to retail load arrangements negotiated under existing 
state-jurisdictional service frameworks. Yet PJM did not vet the details of those definitions 
through a stakeholder process or meaningfully address their effect on already-energized facilities 
and contractual ramp schedules that utilities have studied and agreed to serve.  
PJM has taken its rules for Qualified Facilities and proposed to apply them to retail large 
loads for purposes of siting and sizing, apparently presuming that the same considerations that 
apply to power supply must apply equally to retail load, and that doing so was necessary to 
prevent gaming of the requirements PJM would like to impose on those retail loads. In doing so, 
PJM has strayed into a thicket without a map, threatening to infringe upon existing retail 
contracts and the financial expectations built on them—including retail service contracts for data 
centers that have operated for years or, in many cases, for decades. 
1. A NEW ADDITION DOESN’T MAKE THE WHOLE HOUSE 
NEW: INCREMENTAL LOAD THAT WOULDN’T ITSELF 
COMPRISE A NEW LARGE LOAD SHOULD NOT CAUSE 
EXISTING LOAD TO BE RECATEGORIZED 
Adding a small increment of new load to an existing facility should not recategorize that 
existing load—or the increment itself, if it is below the 50 MW threshold—as a new large load. 
This is especially true where existing contracts already studied and addressed the impacts of the

12 
fully ramped-up project, but it is also true for existing facilities that are not changing their base 
operations or characteristics and are merely adding capacity that would not, on its own, meet the 
definition of “Large Load.”  
That incremental capacity must of course be studied and addressed in the appropriate 
retail service process and contracts, but adding it should not transform a facility that may have 
operated for decades into a “Large Load” itself—potentially disrupting its existing contracts and 
financial expectations, and unnecessarily pulling a small increment of new capacity into the 
IRAS framework when that increment would not, on its own, constitute a new large load. 
 
2. THE WRONG TOOL FOR THE WRONG JOB:  DATA CENTERS 
CANNOT FIT A QF-BASED PROCRUSTEAN BED 
PJM has settled on a one-mile radius to aggregate facilities as a single load entity under 
its definition of Large Load, proposing this rule without regard to existing data center clustering 
practices or the reasons—wholly unrelated to energy—for those practices. Data centers cluster 
for legitimate commercial reasons: locating them near one another creates economic value by 
improving latency, the reliability of data interconnection, and easy access to other customers’ or 
business partners’ computational services, data, networks, and equipment.13 
The one-mile rule can convert incremental growth at a longstanding, separately 
developed group of legacy facilities into “New Large Load” solely because PJM retroactively 
aggregates those facilities into a newly defined single electrical site. In Ashburn’s "Data Center 
Alley," for example, well over a hundred datacenters are located in close proximity. Any one-
mile radius drawn in this area will capture dozens of facilities, many operated by the same 
 
13 See Qualifying Facility Rates and Requirements Implementation Issues Under the Public Utility 
Regulatory Policies Act of 1978, Order No. 872, 172 FERC ¶ 61,041, order on reh’g & clarifying in part, Order No. 
872-A, 173 FERC ¶ 61,158 (2020); IRAS Filing at 33 & n.95.

13 
company and many operated by different companies. Many of those facilities have been 
energized and operational for years or decades. Equinix's first data center in Virginia, DC1, was 
the first commercial data center in that area, and was opened in 1999. That facility is still 
operational, and Equinix has developed numerous additional data centers for within one mile 
over the ensuing decades for data-related and other commercial reasons completely unrelated to 
energy. Many of these facilities are well below 50 MW.  
By combining the one-mile radius with no exception for already-contracted or already-
energized facilities, PJM would retroactively aggregate loads that were separately developed, 
separately studied, and separately contracted for service. The resulting Large Load designation 
could impose new resource-adequacy and curtailment consequences on settled retail 
arrangements. PJM’s anti-gaming rationale does not justify an irrebuttable presumption for 
legacy facilities whose siting decisions predate IRAS and reflect non-energy considerations. 
State regulators and Electric Distributors are better positioned to determine whether separately 
served retail facilities function as a single integrated electrical site. 
PJM should not apply the one-mile aggregation rule to existing, independently developed 
facilities. Affiliated legacy facilities should be evaluated individually unless they were developed 
or are operated as a single integrated electrical site. That determination should turn on electrical 
and operational integration, service arrangements, development history, and applicable state 
rules—not distance alone. The arbitrary results produced by PJM’s proposed definition can be 
seen in three scenarios, each involving 100 MW of otherwise identical load entering service after 
June 1, 2027 and no BYONC or Allocated RBP UCAP MW: 
    •    Scenario 1: Five 20 MW facilities, each more than one mile from the others. 
None individually meets the 50 MW Large Load threshold, and they are not 
aggregated. None is subject to IRAS.

14 
    •    Scenario 2: One 100 MW facility. The facility exceeds the 50 MW 
threshold. The 100 MW is subject to IRAS. 
    •    Scenario 3: Five 20 MW facilities, but three affiliated facilities are within 
the one-mile radius. Those three are aggregated into a 60 MW “single electrical 
site” and therefore meet the Large Load definition. The 60 MW aggregated site is 
subject to IRAS, while the remaining two 20 MW facilities are not. 
The result: Each scenario adds the same 100 MW of load, but PJM's geographic aggregation rule 
produces 0 MW, 100 MW, or 60 MW of IRAS-eligible load, depending solely on how the load is 
physically distributed.   
The distinction illustrated by the examples is particularly egregious when the new load is 
incremental to facilities that are longstanding, independently developed sites whose locations 
predate IRAS, rather than entirely new facilities. 
If PJM retains geographic aggregation for existing facilities, the one-mile rule should 
create a rebuttable presumption, allowing a customer to demonstrate that affiliated facilities are 
separate sites based on factors such as separate service arrangements, points of interconnection, 
development histories, or electrical and operational independence. 
C. YOU BOUGHT IT BUT YOU CAN’T HAVE IT: PJM GETS IT WRONG 
ACCOUNTING FOR NEW LARGE LOADS’ DEMAND-SIDE 
INVESTMENTS 
PJM’s own rules clearly confirm that a Peak Shaving Adjustment reduces the same 
capacity need that BYONC is meant to fill. The IRAS Filing indirectly acknowledges that Peak 
Shaving Adjustments address the same problem as BYONC demand response, in noting that the 
same resource cannot count as both,14 and in adding it to the Large Load Registry.15 Nonetheless, 
the IRAS Filing does not appear to credit the investment a New Large Load may make in a Peak 
 
14 PJM’s own eligibility criteria for demand-side BYONC affirmatively exclude any location that already 
supports a Peak Shaving Adjustment, treating the two mechanisms as mutually exclusive. IRAS Filing at 54. 
15 IRAS Filing at 37, 41.

15 
Shaving Adjustment program, while it explicitly recognizes the comparable investment it may 
make in demand response.16 PJM’s calculation of a New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load 
Amount—the figure that drives that load’s IRAS curtailment exposure—nets out only two 
things: the load’s BYONC arrangements and its Allocated RBP UCAP MW. It does not 
recognize Peak Shaving Adjustments at all – neither as “below the line” credit or as an “above 
the line” deduction, in tax parlance. 
 Under PJM’s proposed calculations, qualifying generation or demand response provided 
through BYONC reduces the amount of a New Large Load that PJM treats as uncovered for 
IRAS purposes. Although that wholesale credit does not itself ensure corresponding protection 
from curtailment or RBP cost allocation under applicable retail rules, PJM at least recognizes the 
resource adequacy value of the qualifying supply and proposes to calculate that value in the 
Large Load Registry. By contrast, PJM provides no credit when a New Large Load funds 
distributed storage or other demand-side capability that qualifies for a Peak Shaving Adjustment, 
even where PJM determines that the adjustment reduces the system’s capacity need by an 
amount comparable to the qualifying supply credited through BYONC. In that circumstance, the 
two investments provide comparable resource adequacy value, one by increasing supply and the 
other by reducing capacity need, but the IRAS calculations would recognize only the former.17,18 
PJM proposes to have the Large Load Registry note, for each Large Load for which it is 
applicable, a “[p]eak shaving adjustment value pursuant to a state program codified in state 
 
16 See, e.g., IRAS Filing at 55-56, 59, 67-68, 86-87. 
17 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, § V(b). 
18 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, § VI(b)(ii)(2); see also IRAS Filing at 54 (explaining that BYONC 
“may be supported by Planned Demand Resource or Planned Distributed Energy Resource . . . Capacity 
Aggregation Resources” only where the underlying location did not previously “reduce the amount of capacity 
needed to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement through a Peak Shaving Adjustment or Price Responsive 
Demand”).

16 
law.”19 But PJM describes that information only as informing operators which Large Loads “are 
managing their resource needs through peak shaving adjustments under a state program.”20 
Because the value is reported for each individual Large Load and described in relation to that 
load’s resource needs, the proposal appears to contemplate only Peak Shaving Adjustments 
associated with the load itself. At minimum, nothing in the proposal allows a New Large Load to 
sponsor incremental peak-shaving capability elsewhere in the same Electric Distributor zone/area 
and receive credit in its IRAS calculation for the resulting reduction in PJM’s capacity need.21,22 
The Large Load Registry field provides information to PJM operators; it does not provide any 
such credit. 
PJM has offered no justification for this asymmetry, and none is apparent. PJM 
recognizes that a qualifying Peak Shaving Adjustment reduces the amount of capacity needed to 
meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement.23 BYONC addresses the same capacity balance 
from the other side by adding qualifying supply. When PJM determines that a Peak Shaving 
Adjustment reduces the capacity need by an amount comparable to the qualifying supply 
credited through BYONC, the two investments provide comparable resource adequacy value. 
Yet Attachment DD-4 credits BYONC and Allocated RBP UCAP MW when calculating a load’s 
Eligible New Large Load Amount, while providing no comparable credit for a qualifying Peak 
Shaving Adjustment. Crediting one form of investment and not the other is not a distinction 
grounded in resource adequacy; it is a distinction grounded in the label PJM has attached to the 
 
19 IRAS Filing at p.43. 
20 IRAS Filing at p.41. 
21 Proposed RAA, Schedule 11, § B.1(a); IRAS Filing at 37. 
22 IRAS Filing at 41 (explaining that the peak shaving adjustment value reported for each Large Load will 
“inform PJM operators of Large Loads that are managing their resource needs through peak shaving adjustments 
under a state program”). 
23 IRAS Filing at 54 (recognizing that a Peak Shaving Adjustment can “reduce the amount of capacity 
needed to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement”); see also Tariff, Attachment DD-2.

17 
mechanism, and is not just and reasonable. 
If the Commission accepts the IRAS proposal, it should at minimum direct PJM to amend 
Attachment DD-4 so that the PJM-determined MW reduction produced by an incremental, 
customer-sponsored Peak Shaving Adjustment reduces the sponsoring load’s Eligible New Large 
Load Amount on a basis comparable to BYONC. The credit should apply whether the qualifying 
capability is located at the sponsoring customer’s site or at another customer’s site, provided the 
reduction is verified, attributable to the sponsoring customer, and protected against double 
counting. This limited revision would recognize that a capacity need can be addressed either by 
adding qualifying supply or by producing a comparable reduction in the amount of capacity PJM 
determines is needed. Without that revision, the proposal is unjust and unreasonable and unduly 
discriminatory or preferential because it imposes different consequences on investments that 
PJM has determined provide comparable resource adequacy value.24 
III.   CONCLUSION 
For the reasons discussed herein, the Commission should reject the IRAS Filing or, at 
minimum, require PJM to: (1) grandfather load and contractual ramps under final retail service 
agreements before August 13, 2026; (2) eliminate or make rebuttable the one-mile aggregation 
rule as applied to independently developed legacy facilities; (3) provide Large Loads notice and 
an opportunity to correct Large Load Registry data before PJM relies on it; and (4) credit the 
PJM-determined value of qualifying, customer-sponsored Peak Shaving Adjustments without 
double counting.
